Look at movies, books, theatre, music- any entertainment. There was always crap mixed with good since the day the medium was invented. Looking back at it's history can be misleading because how we keep track of things have changed.

Before if something wasn't popular few people would own it with no internet to share it with. Eventually it would get thrown away unless a fellow fan spotted it before it was trashed. Eventually the only things that survive are the most popular/well preserved.

Now thanks to the internet, anything that has ever happened can be recorded. As long as the fan has a way to the internet, they can communicate that thing they found/made. At one point you would only know about games that the publisher and market would be comfortable enough to show you in stores. There was tones of crap on the PS2, NES, etc but it probably didn't make it into your country because no one wanted to risk their money on it. For good or bad. Now people can announce when they first start working on a game regardless if it gets finished or not. That stuff happened before, but on a smaller scale, quieter. The many failures hidden.

AAA quality control is purely run by where the money is. GTA5 took £170 million to make. They could pull that off because enough people have proven they will pay the money to play it. There are new sports games every year because enough people buy it. Money encourages behaviour to a product.

Even if Steam dies, indie gaming won't crash. We have places like GOG, itch, humble and such to go to. And more will come, because it's the internet.

Well yeah, you can't trust reviews for AAA titles since there's so much money involved. But indie game reviews are generally more trustworthy. And there's no subjectivity in a gameplay video.

I would make the argument that the market is too cutthroat, which makes an incentive out of cutting corners or making bad games. The indie market is stronger than ever and still EA is releasing buggy games like Assassin's Creed Unity, people still pre-order games knowing or expecting that they will be buggy. The rise of indie gaming, and the hustle of increased competition in the marketplace hasn't really done anything significant to impact any of the "problems" of the games marketplace. The focus is on maximizing profit, which now involves cutting content and shortening release times, nobody is taking any risks or willing to break the chain because they don't want to be left holding a money sinking turd.

It's like arguing that anybody can make a movie, now. You've got video cameras in your cell phones! But making a GOOD movie/game takes significant skill, talent and creativity. It does take a lot of work, and it takes a good team. But the best wont rise to the occasion of the reward isn't worth it.

You have plenty of people who make video games and make them out of love for video games, or love to make video games, but that doesnt mean the finished product will be any good. Some developers take the approach of pricing their game at a much lower point than the other games instead of being innovative or creative to stand out - choosing to capitalize on a high volume of sales rather than putting their heart and time into a game, because there is no guarantee that the game will be successful, or that the game will find an audience.

I would argue that increased competition in the marketplace has driven prices down which is good for consumers economically, but bad for the market. Now the market has moved toward thinner margins (which especially hits indie developers) or free-to-play/"freemium" games, DLC is expected or necessary rather than bonus content, and games have a hard time reaching their audience, even with things like youtube LPs and advertising.

There are more issues I can think of, but I will edit myself since this is getting long. I think of it as the dark shadow of these things that gets ignored until it becomes a problem. Increased competition is good, yes. But there can be too much of a good thing.
